opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a really exciting moment, but I'd describe it as early, more exciting than mature.

There's been a shift from viewing these models as things that answer a question to systems that can pursue a goal. They plan, call tools, write and run code, check their own work, and iterate. That's a meaningful change, and much of the progress has come not from radically new architectures but from composing capabilities: a strong base model, some form of search or planning, access to tools, and, crucially, a way to verify whether the outputs are correct.

That last piece is where I'd put the emphasis. Much of our work in science has taught us that the most powerful agentic systems are the ones paired with a good evaluator. When you can check an answer, for example by running a program, verifying a proof, or simulating a molecule, you can let the system propose many candidates, explore, fail, and improve. The generator gets most of the attention, but the verifier is often what makes the system reliable. Where you lack a crisp signal of correctness, agents get much harder to trust.

I'd point to three open problems. The first is reliability over long horizons. Agents can be impressive for a few steps, but small error rates compound over many steps, so robustness and self-correction matter a lot. The second is memory and state. We need to know how an agent keeps track of what it has learned, what it has tried, and what the world currently looks like, beyond simply stuffing everything into a context window. The third is evaluation. Many of our benchmarks were designed for static question answering, and measuring whether an agent accomplished a real, open-ended task in a messy environment is still quite immature.

Then there are the safety and responsibility questions, which become much sharper once a system can take actions rather than just produce text. Oversight, sandboxing, knowing when to ask a human, all of that needs to be designed in from the start rather than bolted on.

So overall I'm optimistic. Some of the most exciting near-term uses are in domains like mathematics, coding, and scientific discovery, where verification is possible and the payoff from search is large. That's where agents can go beyond assisting us to helping discover things we didn't know.

r002.rationale: The response names reliability, memory and state, evaluation, and safety as open problems, but does not identify the optimal configuration of AI agents as one.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're at an interesting inflection point, where the ideas have matured but the engineering discipline hasn't fully caught up.

For a long time, "agent" meant something fairly narrow in the research community. It meant a policy interacting with an environment, usually trained with reinforcement learning, and the architecture question was mostly about the policy network and the reward. What's changed is that the foundation model has become the core reasoning engine, and the architecture question has shifted to everything around it. How does the model perceive the state of the world? How does it decompose a task? How does it use tools, maintain memory across long horizons, verify its own work, and recover when something goes wrong?

Right now, a lot of the field is treating those as orchestration problems, which is fine as a starting point, but I think the deeper research question is which of those capabilities should live inside the model and which should live in the scaffold. My own view is that the balance keeps shifting toward the model. Things we used to hand-engineer, like explicit planning loops or retrieval heuristics, increasingly get absorbed once you train the model to do them natively. So the scaffolding is often a snapshot of what the model can't yet do on its own.

The second thing I'd highlight is that evaluation is the real bottleneck. We're pretty good at measuring single-turn accuracy. We're much worse at measuring whether an agent behaves reliably over a thousand steps, whether it knows when it's uncertain, whether it fails safely. If you can't measure that, you can't improve it in a principled way, and you end up optimizing for demos rather than robustness.

And the third piece, which I care about a lot, is that the most valuable agents are going to be the ones that operate in domains with ground truth. In science, in mathematics, in code, you can check the output. That lets you close the loop and train the agent on verified outcomes rather than on human preference alone. I think that's where the architecture research and the training research really converge, and where we'll see the most progress over the next couple of years.

r002.rationale: It raises questions about which capabilities belong in the model versus the scaffold, but does not state that finding the optimal configuration of AI agents remains an open research problem.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still very early. We have models with remarkable capabilities, but turning those capabilities into an agent that can reliably accomplish a task over many steps is a different research problem.

An agent needs to plan, interact with an environment, observe what happened, and revise its approach. And it needs some way of assessing whether it’s actually making progress. If a small error goes undetected early on, subsequent steps can compound it. So the question isn’t simply, can the model produce a good plan? It’s, can the system recognize when that plan is wrong and recover?

There are many interesting approaches—using memory, tools, search, or multiple models with different roles. I don’t think we yet know which of those architectural choices are fundamental and which are compensating for limitations of today’s models. That’s an exciting place to be scientifically, but it also means we need careful evaluation of the whole system, especially its reliability over longer tasks.

r002.rationale: It says we do not yet know which architectural choices are fundamental, framing the optimal configuration of AI agents as an open research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at a very exciting stage, but there are still a lot of open questions. We have models that are increasingly capable, and we’re learning how to put them into systems that can use tools, plan, take actions, and learn from feedback. But having a capable model doesn’t automatically give you a reliable agent.

One of the big research questions is how these pieces should fit together. What should the model do directly, and what should be handled by an explicit planning or verification mechanism? How does an agent keep track of what it knows, recognize when it’s made a mistake, and recover? Those questions become particularly important when you move from a short task to something that requires many steps.

So I think there’s a lot of promising experimentation, but I wouldn’t say we’ve converged on a single architecture. The important thing is to evaluate these systems on whether they can reliably accomplish meaningful tasks, including in situations where their initial plan turns out to be wrong.
